models.summary: Five indices under three dimensions, built from fourteen factors. Expenditure is the product of the tertiary share of education spending and the education share of government spending. Enrollment is the gross tertiary rate. Gender equity is one minus the absolute gap between the female-to-male enrollment ratio and the national female-to-male ratio. Research quality is the count of a country's top-500 ARWU universities over its total universities. Internationalization is inbound students over universities. All five are treated as the larger the better.
models.purpose: Compress fourteen factors into five indices that can be scored against each other.
objectives: Produce five comparable indices, one per aspect of the system.

details: India leads on expenditure and trails on research, enrollment and internationalization. Australia leads enrollment at 113 percent.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The indices are reproducible from public data except where the gender formula is ambiguous.

strengths: Each index has a stated meaning and a direction.

limitations: The gender formula is not legible.

assumptions: A higher index always means a healthier system.

models.summary: A TOPSIS-like scoring across countries. The five indices form a matrix, each column is divided by the square root of its sum of squares, and each entry is multiplied by 20 so a perfect country scores 100. The total is the plain sum. There is no ideal solution and no separation measure, so the method is normalization plus scaling, not full TOPSIS. Applied to Australia, India, Japan, Sweden and the United Kingdom for 2017: 53.8, 23.29, 23.54, 48.13, 49.01. India is the lowest and the least balanced, and is chosen.
models.purpose: Rank several countries on one scale and identify the one with the most room to improve.
objectives: Give each country one comparable score and pick the weakest.

identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The ranking is recoverable. The raw matrix is a figure, so the arithmetic cannot be rechecked from the text.

constraints: Countries compared must share one year.
Every index must point the same way.
strengths: A score is only claimed to mean something relative to the others.
The selection rule is explicit: lowest, then least balanced.
limitations: Called TOPSIS but drops the ideal point and the distance.
Equal weight per index is never justified.

models.summary: The same scoring run down a time axis. India's five indices at successive dates, including the predicted dates after each five-year plan, form the matrix and are normalized and scaled exactly as in the crosswise model. The path judges whether the system moves toward the vision. Fed with the plan targets, the total rises from 24.79 in 2017 to 57.96 in 2037. Note the 2017 figure differs from the 23.29 of the crosswise run, because the comparison group is now a set of years rather than a set of countries.
models.purpose: Score the present and the planned future on one scale and read the trend.
objectives: Show the score at each date and confirm the plans raise it.

algorithm.description: Insert the target values, normalize down each index, scale, sum, read the path.

details: Total score from 24.79 in 2017 to 57.96 in 2037. Enrollment, internationalization and research rise each period.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The endpoints are printed. The intermediate scores live in figures, and the 2017 value disagrees with the crosswise score.

constraints: Same five indices and same scaling as the crosswise model.
Future rows are plans, so the score measures the plan, not a forecast.
strengths: The plan is judged by the same instrument as the diagnosis.
The change of comparison group is visible in the shifted 2017 score.
limitations: Scoring targets against the present makes the rise nearly automatic.
The two 2017 scores are never reconciled.
missing_details: The target value of each index at each date.
assumptions: A rising score means movement toward the vision.

models.summary: Four targets over four five-year plans from 2017. Enrollment: the top 30 percent of the population reaches Australia's 113 percent, while the lower 70 percent reaches k times that, with k equal to 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 across the four plans, giving an expected rate of (0.3 + 0.7k) times 113 percent. Ranked universities: 5, 8, 9, then 7 new entries into the top 500. Inbound students grow 7 percent a year, then 11 percent, then fluctuate around 5 percent. Universities are cut by half in the first plan.
models.purpose: Turn the three weak indices into dated numerical targets.
objectives: Set a target the vertical model can score.

Population share treated as the upper group, 0.3
Fraction of the benchmark the lower group reaches in plan p: 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4
Expected national enrollment rate in plan p

governing_equations.purpose: Upper group at the benchmark, lower group at a rising fraction of it.

equation_status.note: The weighted form is printed in prose. The other three targets are schedules, not equations.

details: Base year 2017. Lower castes and the excluded group taken as 70 percent of population.
k capped at 0.4, so the lower group never passes 40 percent of the benchmark within the horizon.

parameter_estimation.method: The fractions and the university counts are chosen after reading comparable countries. No fitting.

algorithm.description: Fix the benchmark from the best country, discount it for the lower group, and step the discount up each plan.

details: Enrollment target (0.3 + 0.7k) times 113 percent. New top-500 entries: 5, 8, 9, 7. Inbound growth 7, 11, then about 5 percent a year. Universities halved in five years.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The enrollment target is computable. The university and student targets are round numbers without a derivation.

constraints: Benchmark taken from the five-country set only.
University merger assumed two-into-one for the middle 40 percent.
strengths: The enrollment target is tiered instead of applied flat to a divided population.
The early-fast-then-slow shape of the ranking target is given a reason.
limitations: Halving the universities in five years is assumed feasible.
missing_details: The current enrollment rate the target is measured against.
assumptions: The top 30 percent can reach the Australian rate.
Ranked-university growth slows as the bar bites.
